MIZORAM PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
COMPETITIVE EXAMINATION (COMBINED TECHNICAL) FOR
RECRUITMENT TO THE POSTS OF AGRICULTURE & ALLIED SERVICES,
GOVERNMENT OF MIZORAM.
(NOVEMBER-2025)
GENERAL ENGLISH
Time Allowed : 3 hours
FM : 100
SECTION - A (Conventional Type) (50 Marks)
This Section should be answered only on the Answer Sheet provided.
Marks for each question is indicated against it.
1. Write a Precis of the given passage, condensing it to approximately one third of the original length
and give a title for the same.
(15)
Morality constitutes the invisible framework that upholds the ethical foundation of any society,
governing the conduct of individuals and shaping the collective conscience of a civilization. It transcends
mere legality or convention, embodying the intrinsic sense of right and wrong that determines the
moral tenor of human interactions. A society’s moral fabric is neither static nor universal; it evolves in
response to cultural, religious, and philosophical influences, reflecting the values and principles its
people deem essential for harmonious coexistence. Without a moral compass to guide human behaviour,
even the most sophisticated social structures risk descending into chaos and ethical decay.
The vitality of morality lies in its capacity to generate mutual trust and social cohesion.
Moral principles such as honesty, compassion, integrity, and justice serve as the cornerstones of
cooperative living, enabling individuals to interact with respect and empathy. When citizens adhere to
shared ethical norms, society achieves a sense of unity and purpose greater than the sum of its parts.
Conversely, when morality erodes under the pressure of materialism, corruption, or moral relativism,
social divisions deepen, and institutions lose their legitimacy. In this sense, morality functions as both
the glue and the safeguard of civilization.
Throughout history, moral thought has been shaped by various philosophical traditions and
religious doctrines. From the Aristotelian notion of virtue ethics to Kant’s categorical imperative and
the utilitarian emphasis on the greatest good for the greatest number, thinkers have sought to define
the basis of moral responsibility. These philosophical foundations continue to influence modern ethical
discourse, guiding laws, education, and interpersonal relations. Despite cultural diversity, the universal
aspiration toward moral goodness underscores humanity’s innate desire for justice and compassion,
attesting to the moral continuity that binds civilizations across time and geography.
In contemporary society, advances in technology, globalization, and social media have posed
new moral dilemmas that challenge traditional ethical frameworks. Issues such as data privacy, artificial
intelligence, climate responsibility, and social inequality demand a reevaluation of moral standards in
light of modern complexity. The pace of change often outstrips the development of moral consensus,
leaving individuals and institutions grappling with ambiguous ethical choices. As a result, the need for
moral reflection and education becomes ever more urgent, not merely as a social requirement but as
a condition for the preservation of human dignity in an increasingly impersonal world.

- 2 -
Ultimately, morality serves as the spiritual and ethical compass of society, directing collective
progress toward justice and human flourishing. It reminds individuals that true advancement lies not
only in material prosperity but in the cultivation of virtue and the pursuit of truth. A morally grounded
society fosters empathy over exploitation, fairness over greed, and altruism over selfish ambition.
When guided by moral integrity, civilization ascends beyond mere survival to achieve a higher form of
human excellence—one in which wisdom, virtue, and conscience define the essence of progress.
2. Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow:
Economic inequality, a condition deeply entrenched in many modern societies, has become
a pressing concern for both policymakers and scholars. This imbalance, evident in the unequal allocation
of wealth and resources, frequently intensifies social divisions and poses substantial obstacles to fair
access to opportunities. Such widespread disparity undermines the core pillars of social unity, making
the goal of shared prosperity ever more difficult to achieve.
Over time, a multitude of factors have driven economic inequality, ranging from colonial
exploitation and uneven globalization to unpredictable fiscal policies. These historical influences have
combined to create entrenched socioeconomic structures in which the affluent elite hold excessive
sway over political and economic decisions. As a consequence, marginalized populations are often
consigned to living in subsistence conditions, deprived of vital infrastructural resources.
In contemporary contexts, technological advancement and capital markets have paradoxically
fostered both unprecedented growth and deepening inequality. The ascendancy of automation, though
ostensibly designed to enhance efficiency, has often displaced swathes of the labour force, thereby
aggravating unemployment rates. At the same time, the expansion of speculative investment opportunities
has further benefited individuals with existing wealth, deepening the divide between the rich and the
poor.
One cannot overlook the insidious ramifications of economic inequality on democratic
institutions. When affluence confers outsized political leverage, public policy risks becoming skewed
towards the preservation of privilege rather than the redress of injustice. This distortion undermines
the legitimacy of governance, fostering cynicism amongst the disenfranchised and imperiling societal
stability.
Addressing economic inequality necessitates a multifaceted approach encompassing
progressive taxation, expansive educational access, and robust social welfare mechanisms. Reforms
must transcend mere palliative measures, aspiring instead towards the dismantlement of entrenched
inequities. Only through such deliberate and comprehensive intervention may societies envisage a
future wherein prosperity is both shared and sustainable.
(a) Define ‘economic inequality’ as portrayed in the passage.
(2)
(b) Identify two historical factors mentioned that have contributed to economic disparity.
(2)
(c) Explain how automation has paradoxically affected economic inequality.
(2)
(d) Find the antonym of the word ‘temporary’ from the passage.
(1)
(e) Find the synonym of the word ‘wealthy’ from the passage.
(1)
(f) Make sentences using the word ‘overlook’ both as a noun and as a verb.
(1+1=2)

Notes regarding Negative Marking :
(i) There will be penalty (negative marking) for every wrong answer given by a candidate in the MCQ
type questions.
(ii) For each question for which a wrong answer has been given by the candidate, one-third of the
marks assigned to that question will be deducted as penalty
(iii) If a candidate gives more than one answer to one question, it will be treated as a wrong answer even
if any one of the given answers happens to be correct and there will be same penalty as above for
that question.
(iv) If a question is left blank, i.e., no answer is given by the candidate, there will be no penalty for that
question.

MIZORAM PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
TECHNICAL COMPETITIVE EXAMINATION FOR
JUNIOR GRADE OF MIZORAM HEALTH SERVICES (COMBINED) UNDER
HEALTH & FAMILY WELFARE DEPARTMENT,
GOVERNMENT OF MIZORAM.
 (SEPTEMBER-2025)
GENERAL ENGLISH
Time Allowed : 3 hours
FM : 100
SECTION - A
(60 Marks)
The questions in this Section should be answered only on the Answer Sheet provided.
Marks are indicated against each question.
1. Write an essay on any one of the following:
(20)
(a) The role of family in creating a well-adjusted society
(b) Physical health leads to mental health
(c) Hospital acquired infection- Prevention and Control.
2. Write a precis of the following passage. Supply a suitable title:
(20)
It is physically impossible for a well-educated, intellectual or brave man to make money the
chief object of his thoughts just as it is for him to make his dinner the principal object of them. All
healthy people like their dinners, but their dinner is not the main object of their lives.
So all healthy minded people like making money ought to like it and enjoy the sensation of
winning it; it is something better than money. A good soldier, for instance, mainly wishes to do his
fighting well. He is glad of his pay very properly so, and justly grumbles when you keep him ten years
without it-still his main mission of life is to win battles, not to be paid for winning them. So of clergymen.
The clergyman’s object is essentially baptize and preach not to be paid for preaching. So of doctors.
They like fees no doubt—ought to like them; yet if they are brave and well-educated, the entire
object to their lives is not fees. They, on the whole, desire to cure the sick; and if they are good
doctors and the choice were fairly to them, would rather cure their patient and lose their fee than kill
him and get it. And so, with all the other brave and rightly trained men: their work is first, their fee
second—very important always; but still second.

- 2 -
Direction (Question Nos. 3 - 12) : Read the passage, and answer the questions based on the given
passage. Marks are indicated against each question.
A person who takes the trouble to form his own opinions and beliefs, will feel that he owes no
responsibility to the majority for his conclusions. If he is a genuine lover of truth, if he is inspired by a
passion for seeing things as they are and an abhorrence of holding ideas which do not conform to
facts, he will be wholly independent of the assent of those around him. When he proceeds to apply
his beliefs in the practical conduct of life, the position is different. There are then good reasons why
his attitude should be less inflexible. The society in which he is placed is an ancient and composite
growth. The people from whom he dissents have not come by their opinions, customs and by a
process of mere haphazard.
These opinions and customs all have their origin in a certain real supposed fitness. They have
certain depth of root in the lives of a proportion of the existing generation. Their congruity with one
another may have come to an end. That is only one side of the truth. The most zealous propagandism
cannot penetrate to them. In common language, we speak of a generation as something possessed of
a kind of exact unity, with all its parts and members homogenous. Yet, plainly it is not this. It is a
whole but a whole in a state of constant flux its factors and elements are eternally shifting. It is not one
but many generations.
Each of the seven ages of man is neighbour to all the rest. The column of the veterans is already
sinking into the last abyss, while the column of the newest recruits is forming to its tradition, its
tendency and its possibilities. Only a proportion of each can have nerve enough to grasp the banner
of a new truth and endurance to bear it along rugged and untrodden ways. Thus, we must remember
the stuff of which life is made.
We must consider what an over whelming preponderance of the most tenacious energies and
most concentrated interest of a society must be absorbed between material cares and the solitude of
the affections.
It is obviously unreasonable to lose patience and quarrel with one’s time because it is tardy in
throwing off its institution and beliefs and slow to achieve the transformation which is the problem in
front of it. Men and women have to live.
The task for most of us is arduous enough to make us well pleased with even such imperfect
shelter as we find in daily use and won’t.
To insist on whole community being made at once to submit to the reign of new practices and
ideas that have just begun to commend themselves to the most advance speculative intelligence of the
time, this even if it were a possible process, would do hurry on special dissolution.
